subject: Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model

messages.author: 07019e4ee91b7432
messages.subject: Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
Hi Stan Users,

I've encountered a mild identification issue using HMC/stan that has never been an issue using ML in commercial software. I'm looking for advice about the best way to solve it. 

I am estimating a factor analysis model with 2 correlated factors and 10 binary indicators (this can also be a multidimensional item response theory model). I've attached the model in stan and an example data set simulated from the model. The scale of the factors/latent variables is set to N(0,1). The parameters to be estimated are 10 intercepts and factor loadings for each of the 10 items and the correlation between factors. In the generating model, the thresholds are 0 and the factor loadings and correlation between factors are all positive. 

When I estimate the model using ML, the estimates are all positive. When I run the model in stan, half of the time all of the parameters are positive and I get the same result as ML. The other half of the time, the solution is half-reflected: positive loadings on one factor, negative loadings on the other factor, and a negative correlation between factors. If I run the model with 5 chains, the aggregated result is worthless because all of the estimates average to zero. I haven't seen a switch between solutions within a single chain, so I don't know if that is also something I should worry about. These two solutions are likelihood equivalent, but the split negative/positive solution never comes up in common SEM software (e.g. Mplus). I don't know why this problem never comes up in Mplus (they aren't very transparent), but the split negative/positive solution also isn't preferred for interpretation. 

Are there any suggestions about avoiding the split negative/positive solution in stan? I can see doing:
A) switching the signs as a post-processing step
B) choosing starting values to start the chains in the desired neighborhood

My first thought was (A), but I wasn't sure if that is frowned upon. Should starting values help? Are there other ideas? I do not want to constrain any of the parameters to be positive, because with different data negative parameter values would be acceptable. I also want to avoid tightening the priors for this reason, this is supposed to be a very general model.

I used the following code in R to read in the data and fit the model:
dat<-read.table("data1.dat", header=FALSE)
N<-500 #observations

K<-10   #items
F<-2     #factors
cfa.data<-list(N=N,K=K,F=F,y=dat)

#compile model
    model=rstan::stan_model(file="cfa2factor.stan")

#evaluate model
    out=rstan::sampling(object = model
        , data=cfa.data
        , chains=5
        , iter=10000
        , warmup=Niter/2
        , refresh=Niter/10)

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
Can you constrain certain of the parameters to be positive to break the aliasing?  Also, typically we don’t need 10,000 iterations.  If it takes that many iterations, it can typicallly be worth it to reparameterize in some way.  Also I think there should be a better way for you to parameterize this multivariate normal dist, but I’m no exeprt on that, maybe someone else on list can help.
A

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
On Sunday, January 31, 2016 at 9:05:53 PM UTC-5, Sierra wrote:
When I run the model in stan, half of the time all of the parameters are positive and I get the same result as ML. The other half of the time, the solution is half-reflected: positive loadings on one factor, negative loadings on the other factor, and a negative correlation between factors. If I run the model with 5 chains, the aggregated result is worthless because all of the estimates average to zero. I haven't seen a switch between solutions within a single chain, so I don't know if that is also something I should worry about. These two solutions are likelihood equivalent, but the split negative/positive solution never comes up in common SEM software (e.g. Mplus). I don't know why this problem never comes up in Mplus (they aren't very transparent), but the split negative/positive solution also isn't preferred for interpretation.

Commercial software and factanal() in R will often post-process the MLE in some way to resolve the sign indeterminacy (you can multiply the factors by -1 and multiply the loadings by -1 and get the same linear predictor).

Are there any suggestions about avoiding the split negative/positive solution in stan? I can see doing:
A) switching the signs as a post-processing step
In this case (but not always), that is logically fine, although the presence of multiple modes may undermine the sampler.
B) choosing starting values to start the chains in the desired neighborhood

This won't help much.

The best option, in this case, would be

C)  Constrain cov to be either positive (or negative) with

real <lower=0, upper=1> cov;

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
Thanks Ben. Because the covariance could be negative with different data, I think I will have to post-process the solutions where this arises. The issue is I don't want BOTH a negative covariance AND all negative loadings on one factor. But in isolation, negative loadings or a negative covariance would be acceptable.

I just hope the sign doesn't switch within a chain. From what I have seen, the sampler hones in on one mode quickly and stays there, but that doesn't rule out the possibility that the sampler could switch around.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts: But in isolation, negative loadings or a negative covariance would be acceptable.

Right, but because of the sign non-identifiabiltiy there is always an equivalence.
If you enforce positive corrections then you can always “recover” negative ones
by flipping the total sign, and likewise for the loadings.  To enforce identifiability
you have to force either the loadings or the correlations to be positive (the
correlations are straightforward to enforce as Ben notes) and then figure out
how you want to interpret them.  Any post processing would be doing the same
thing.

messages.author: f3947cd9f9a85fbd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
Taking a step backward, there are two ways to identify the latent factors:
A) set mean to 0 and variance to 1
B) scale each factor by setting a single indicator to 1 (mean still 0)

As we can see, A has this sign indeterminacy problem. If I switch the scaling to B, I believe the identification problem goes away, and I can look at standardized estimates to get the preferred interpretation. 

I find it interesting that a very commonly used model is only locally identified, but the "standard" software doesn't let on to the indeterminacy.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
On Monday, February 1, 2016 at 9:47:48 AM UTC-5, Sierra Bainter wrote:
Thanks Ben. Because the covariance could be negative with different data, I think I will have to post-process the solutions where this arises. The issue is I don't want BOTH a negative covariance AND all negative loadings on one factor. But in isolation, negative loadings or a negative covariance would be acceptable.

You could have a negative covariance with the current data. The identification issue that there are a set of loadings that go with a positive covariance that produce the same likelihood of the data as another set of loadings that go with a negative covariance. It doesn't particularly matter which one you pick, but you will get much more efficient sampling from Stan if you pick one or the other. Otherwise, different chains could concentrate around different modes or a chain could switch modes during sampling.

In the two factor case, constraining the sign of the factor covariances is easier than constraining the sign of two of the loadings or two of the factors. But that doesn't really generalize to the 3+ factor case.

Ben

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
hi sierra,  you probably know that rotational and reflection (which may also be viewed as a rotation) non-identifiability is inherent to the factor analytic construction.  under MLE (where a prior is not assigned), it is relatively easy to fix an arbitrary rotation that will rotationally identify the loadings and factors (see Mardia, Kent and Bibbie).   one may subsequently apply optimized rotations (e.g. varimax) for inference.   (there are also scale and location non-identifiabilities. the former is resolved, as you note, by setting the prior variance on the factors to 1.   the latter is solved by excluding an intercept).   under a bayesian setting - with priors assigned to the loadings - it is non-trivial to fix a rotation to separately rotationally identify the loadings and factors.   until recently, one used the approach suggested by Geweke that fixes a rotation by restricting the loadings matrix to lower triangular with positive diagonals.  you may readily use this approach in JAGS or Stan.  In the former, mixing is improved by introducing redundant scale parameters (a la Gelman).  Such is not needed or advisable in Stan.   

while fixing the rotation of the loadings matrix using Geweke will fully resolve the multimodality, it induces a non-exchangeable prior on the loadings. this prior non-exchangeability results in sensitivity of the estimated posterior distributions on the loadings to the order in which the variables are listed in your data, which is a highly undesirable property.    there are many recently developed methods that all perform sampling without any rotational (including sign) restrictions on the loadings and use post-processing steps to recover identifiability, as was mentioned in earlier responses.  this has been a very active area of research over the past 5 - 7 years.   i attach a paper of mine that comments on a number of these methods and provides references.  the paper also includes a new method to achieve identifiability in post-processing that is more straightforward to understand, makes no assumptions on the true structure of the loadings matrix and is easier to implement than those listed.  i may publish software to implement it, down-the-road, if there is interest.  That said, it should be very easy to just do this, yourself, in R. Since the publication of this paper Veronika Rockova also has an approach you might want to check out.

all to say, i recommend against attempting to constrain parameters to achieve identifiability during sampling.

Hi Terrance, yes the issue of rotational non-identifiability is as old as factor analysis. Fortunately, this is a confirmatory model, so rotation does not come into play in the same way as with exploratory factor analysis. 

Changing the scaling for the latent factors (by scaling to an indicator), as I proposed in my last post, resolves the sign indeterminacy for this model.

while fixing the rotation of the loadings matrix using Geweke will fully resolve the multimodality, it induces a non-exchangeable prior on the loadings. this prior non-exchangeability results in sensitivity of the estimated posterior distributions on the loadings to the order in which the variables are listed in your data, which is a highly undesirable property.    there are many recently developed methods that all perform sampling without any rotational (including sign) restrictions on the loadings and use post-processing steps to recover identifiability, as was mentioned in earlier responses.  this has been a very active area of research over the past 5 - 7 years.   i attach a paper of mine that comments on a number of these methods and provides references.  the paper also includes a new method to achieve identifiability in post-processing that is more straightforward to understand, makes no assumptions on the true structure of the loadings matrix and is easier to implement than those listed.  i may publish software to implement it, down-the-road, if there is interest.  That said, it should be very easy to just do this, yourself, in R. Since the publication of this paper Veronika Rockova also has an approach you might want to check out.

all to say, i recommend against attempting to constrain parameters to achieve identifiability during sampling.


On Mon, Feb 1, 2016 at 10:15 AM, Sierra Bainter <sierra....@gmail.com> wrote:
Taking a step backward, there are two ways to identify the latent factors:
A) set mean to 0 and variance to 1
B) scale each factor by setting a single indicator to 1 (mean still 0)

As we can see, A has this sign indeterminacy problem. If I switch the scaling to B, I believe the identification problem goes away, and I can look at standardized estimates to get the preferred interpretation. 

I find it interesting that a very commonly used model is only locally identified, but the "standard" software doesn't let on to the indeterminacy. 

On Mon, Feb 1, 2016 at 10:01 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

But in isolation, negative loadings or a negative covariance would be acceptable.

Right, but because of the sign non-identifiabiltiy there is always an equivalence.
If you enforce positive corrections then you can always “recover” negative ones
by flipping the total sign, and likewise for the loadings.  To enforce identifiability
you have to force either the loadings or the correlations to be positive (the
correlations are straightforward to enforce as Ben notes) and then figure out
how you want to interpret them.  Any post processing would be doing the same
thing.

--

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
This has been super helpful for me, so thanks for
all the comments everyone. I just wanted to add one
more thing:

Often, you don't care about identifiability of the parameters
so much as identifiability of the inferences you make with them.
In the simple case of a mixture of two normals, we get a label
switching problem if we don't somehow identify them in the prior.
But, if all we want to do is event probability estimation or
posterior predictive inference, it doesn't matter --- the identification
issue goes away.

Having said this, it can help for the sampling algorithm to be
more constrained. Which is why we almost always recommend trying
to identify the parameters of the model itself, not just the
downstream inferences for quantities of interest.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mild identification/label switching issue for categorical factor analysis model
parts:
Stan doesn't know anything about models other than
how to load their data and then evaluate their density
and gradients.

- Bob
